doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Technology: two linked 16-track machines and mixing with Gene Paul
summary: Dorn claims to be first to link two 16-track machines. He describes his current studio with Gene Paul and mixing analog and digital.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah. Technology changed I think considerably in your producing career and still is. Was the advent of having more tracks to work with —

I invented more tracks. And I’m going to tell you the one thing I did that had to do with technology. I was the first person to hook two 16-track tape machines together. Because sometimes I was so nuts there were just never enough tracks.

I was an overdub junkie. And so a guy by the name of Bob Lifton, an engineer I work with, he found a piece of equipment that could tie the two machines together. I almost got fired from Atlantic when I did that because I experimented a little bit, I might have spent an extra couple of dollars. But then the whole industry turned to that. I made another enemy in-house. The technology changes. Maybe I’ll shortcut your question. It doesn’t really make a lot of difference whether something is on a 78 or an MP3. I make content. I don’t care what they do with it. In other words if I had my choice I would work with two 16-track machines on two inch tape. And then I would transfer that to a digital form. Now I just go directly into Pro Tools.
Are you one of those people who say that there’s something missing from the analog?

There is something missing from a certain part of the analog recordings but at that little studio that you were in we have our own way of making digital sound like analog. You saw what we did. You know, so we have all that cutting edge equipment on the right and all the shit we stole from Atlantic on the left when the studio closed. We got all those limiters and compressors and out of print pieces of equipment. And Gene really knows what he’s doing. He’s Les Paul’s kid. He grew up in the house where most of this was invented. You know it’s like putting a light bulb in a socket and with Edison’s kid doing the turning. So we’ve got a way to do it.
